summary: This unit teaches you to choose, check and use marking out tools, so that parts are cut, drilled and fitted in exactly the right place. You will learn to work from a drawing and a datum, mark lines, angles, circles and hole centres on metal with scribers, squares, dividers and punches, and set out level, plumb and square lines on walls and floors on site. You will also learn to check your marking, look after the tools and report problems.

blocks.p: **Marking out** means transferring the sizes and shapes on a drawing onto the material or the building, so that cutting, drilling, bending and fixing happen in the right place. Every later step depends on it: a part marked wrongly is cut wrongly, however good the cutting.

**Who it is for:** this unit is shared by the Welding and Fabrication and the Electrical Installation programmes at Level 2. Welders and fabricators mark out plates, bars and sections in the workshop. Electricians mark out positions for boxes, conduit, trunking and fixings on walls, ceilings and floors. Both use the same principles: work from the drawing, measure from a datum, use sharp, accurate tools, and check before you cut or drill.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Plan the marking out
Read the drawing and job sheet, check the material, choose datum edges or lines, and plan the layout to save material.
Work safely
Control sharp points, flying chips, sharp edges, heavy sheets, flammable marking dye, lasers and hidden cables and pipes.
Choose and check the tools
Pick the right measuring, marking, squaring and punching tools for the job and surface, and check that each is accurate and in good condition.
Prepare the surface
Clean and deburr the material and apply marking dye, or choose a marker that suits the surface.
Mark lines, angles, circles and centres
Scribe lines from a datum; mark squares and angles; find centres; scribe circles and hole positions, including holes on a pitch circle.
Punch accurately
Prick punch and centre punch hole centres exactly on line crossings; add witness marks.
Mark out on site
Set out level, plumb and straight lines and square corners on walls and floors, and check for hidden services.
Check, store and report
Check every size against the drawing, correct mistakes, care for and store the tools, and report damage.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on planning, safety, choosing and checking tools, measuring, datums, surface preparation, punching, circles and centres, angles, surface plate work, allowances, site marking, checking, templates and tool care.
A **written paper** with short answers (tool names, punch angles, kerf, simple sums) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Practical tasks**: marking out and punching a steel template plate from a drawing, and setting out fixing positions on a practice wall board and a square rectangle on the floor.

blocks.note: Short-answer questions ask for exact names: scriber, prick punch, centre punch, transfer punch, dividers, trammel, odd-leg calipers, spirit level, plumb bob, chalk line, datum, kerf and burr.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Before you mark out: drawings, datums, material and safety

flow: Check the drawing is for this job and is the latest revision
Read the title block and notes: material, thickness, units (usually mm), tolerance and quantity
Study the views and find every size you will need
Find the datum edges or lines the sizes are measured from
Get the material and check its type, size and condition
Plan where each part will go on the plate or sheet
Ask the supervisor about anything missing or unclear

ul: Sizes on the drawing are in **millimetres** unless it says otherwise: 1250 on a drawing means 1250 mm, which is 1.25 m. Older drawings and some tapes use inches: 1 inch = 25.4 mm.
**Ø** in front of a size means diameter (Ø18 is a hole 18 mm across). Holes are positioned by their **centre lines**: thin chain lines (long and short dashes) through the middle of each hole.
The material and thickness are in the **title block** or the **notes**.
Never measure the drawing itself to find a size: work from the written dimensions.

blocks.p: A **datum** is the edge, line or point that all sizes are measured from. In the workshop it is usually two straight, clean edges at 90° to each other, or a centre line. On site it may be a level line on the wall, the finished floor level, or a gridline.

ul: Measure **every** size from the datum, not from the last mark. If you measure each hole from the one before, small errors add up along the row; from a datum, each error stays small.
Choose datum edges that are straight and square. File off burrs so the square and rule sit true against them.
Use the same datums the drawing uses. If the drawing dimensions from the left edge, so do you.
Mark the datum edges (for example with a small "D") so everyone uses the same ones.
Place parts on the sheet or bar so that little material is wasted (this is called **nesting**).
Use a straight factory edge as a datum where you can, so you have one less cut to make.
Allow for the width of each cut between parts (the **kerf**) and for any machining or finishing allowance the drawing gives.

head: Hazard
Control
rows: Sharp scriber, divider and trammel points
Keep caps or corks on the points; never carry them in a pocket; pass them handle first
Chips flying when punching; mushroomed punch heads
Safety glasses; never use a punch with a mushroomed head until it is dressed
Sharp edges and burrs on cut steel
Deburr edges; wear gloves to handle plate and sheet
Heavy sheets and plates
Lift with your legs, get help or use a trolley; keep fingers clear when laying sheets down
Marking dye: flammable, gives off vapour
Use with good air flow; keep the lid on; keep it away from heat, sparks and flames
Steel tapes snapping back
Let the blade wind in slowly; the edge can cut
Hidden cables and pipes in walls and floors
Check drawings and use a detector before drilling or fixing
Laser levels
Never look into the beam or point it at anyone's eyes
Working at height; trip hazards on site
Keep marks within safe reach or use proper access; keep tapes and lines out of walkways

sections.title: Measuring tools and keeping them accurate

head: Tool
What it is for
Good practice
rows: Steel rule (150 mm, 300 mm, 600 mm, 1 m)
Measuring and marking straight lines; setting dividers and calipers
Stand it on its edge so the graduations touch the work
Look **straight down** at the mark: looking from the side gives a wrong reading (parallax)
Graduations are usually in 1 mm and 0.5 mm
Tape measure
Longer lengths, in the workshop and on site
The hook slides by its own thickness, so readings are true whether it is hooked on or pushed against a wall
Read the metric edge: many tapes also show inches
Do not let the blade snap back or kink
Combination set
A rule with interchangeable heads
**Square head**: lines at 90° and 45°, often with a spirit level and a small scriber
**Centre head**: finds the centre of round bar
**Protractor head**: lines at any angle
Vernier or digital caliper
Measuring thickness, diameters and hole sizes accurately (often to 0.02 mm or 0.01 mm)
Close the jaws to check zero; keep it in its case

blocks.h: Checking that your tools are accurate

head: Tool
Check
If it fails
rows: Try square or engineer's square
Hold the stock against a straight edge and scribe a line; turn the square over and scribe again from the same point. The two lines should lie on top of each other.
If they spread apart, the square is out of true: do not use it; label and report it
Steel rule
Look at the end: is it square, sharp and undamaged?
If the end is worn or bent, measure from the 10 mm line and take 10 mm off the reading, and report it
Tape measure
Check the hook is not bent and the rivets are not worn; compare a reading with a steel rule
Replace a tape with a bent hook or kinked blade
Spirit level
Read the bubble on a surface, turn the level end for end on the same spot and read again: the bubble should sit the same
If not, it needs adjusting or replacing
Scriber, divider and punch points
Sharp, and the right shape
Have them sharpened by a competent person

blocks.note: A small knock can spoil a square or rule for good. Never use one as a lever, a hammer or a screwdriver, and never drop it or throw other tools on top of it.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Tool
Use
Good practice
rows: Scriber
Scratching a fine, clear line on metal
Keep the point sharp: a blunt point makes a wide line that is less accurate
Lean it so the point runs tight in the corner between rule and work
One firm stroke; do not go over and over the line
Marking blue (layout dye)
Coating bright metal so scribed lines show up clearly
Clean off dirt, grease and loose rust first
One thin, even coat; let it dry
Flammable: lid on, away from heat and sparks, good air flow
Soapstone (French chalk)
Marking dark steel, and steel to be flame cut or welded
Stays visible when the steel gets hot; sharpen it to a flat edge for a thin line
Paint marker or metal-marking pencil
Clear lines on black, rusty or galvanised steel, stainless steel and aluminium
Choose one made for metal; keep lines thin
Pencil
Walls, timber, board; light marks on coated metal
Sharp point; mark lightly where the mark must be removed later
Chalk line
Long straight lines on walls, floors and large sheets
Blue or white chalk washes off; some coloured chalks stain permanently

blocks.h: Choosing a marking method for the surface

head: Surface
Best way to mark
Why
rows: Bright mild steel (cleaned, ground or machined)
Marking blue and a scriber
Gives the finest, most accurate lines
Black hot-rolled steel with mill scale
Soapstone, paint marker or metal-marking pencil; centre punch witness marks along cut lines
A scratch hardly shows on scale, and ink burns off in gas cutting
Steel to be flame or plasma cut
Soapstone, with punch witness marks
Soapstone survives the heat; punch marks stay if the line burns off
Galvanised sheet
Pencil or fine marker (scribe only on the waste side)
A scratch cuts through the zinc and lets rust start
Aluminium sheet
Fine marker or pencil, especially on bend lines
A scratch on a bend line can start a crack when it is folded
Painted wall or plaster
Pencil, marked lightly; chalk line for long lines
A scratch or ink would spoil the finish
Concrete floor or slab
Chalk line, crayon or marker
Shows clearly and is easy to see while working

blocks.note: In a humid workshop, bright steel starts to rust within hours, and rust lifts the dye and hides the lines. Clean and mark close to the time you will cut, and keep marked parts dry.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Tool
Use
rows: Try square or engineer's square
Marking and checking lines at 90° to an edge
Combination set square head
Lines at 90° and 45°; also measuring depths
Protractor (or protractor head)
Marking and measuring any angle, such as 30° or 60°
Sliding bevel
Copying an angle from one part and transferring it to another

head: Tool
Use
Good practice
rows: Dividers
Scribing circles and arcs; stepping off equal distances
Set to the **radius**, half the diameter: for a Ø120 circle, set 60 mm
Set them on a rule's graduation lines, for example from the 10 mm line to the 70 mm line
Put a light punch mark at the centre for the fixed leg to sit in
Trammel (beam compass)
Circles and arcs too large for dividers
Two pointed heads clamped on a beam or bar
Odd-leg (jenny) calipers
Scribing lines parallel to an edge; finding the rough centre of a bar
Run the bent leg along a clean edge; hold the scribing point square

blocks.h: Finding the centre of a round bar

ul: **Centre head:** sit the bar's end in the centre head's V, scribe a line along the rule's edge, turn the bar about a quarter turn and scribe again. Where the lines cross is the centre.
**Odd-leg calipers:** set them to about the radius and scribe four short arcs from points spaced round the edge. The centre is in the middle of the small shape the arcs make; mark it and check.
A **bell punch** (centre-finding punch) has a bell-shaped body that sits over the bar's end and centres its point.

blocks.p: Flanges and covers often have holes **equally spaced** on a circle called the **pitch circle diameter (PCD)**. The angle between hole centres is **360° ÷ the number of holes**: 4 holes are 90° apart, 6 holes 60°, 8 holes 45°.

flow: Scribe two centre lines at 90° and lightly punch the centre
Set the dividers to half the PCD and scribe the pitch circle
Mark the first hole where the circle crosses a centre line
Step round with dividers set to the chord between holes, or mark the angles with a protractor
Check that the last step lands exactly on the first mark; if it does not, adjust the dividers slightly and step round again
Prick punch, check, then centre punch each hole centre

head: Number of holes
Angle apart
Chord between neighbours
rows: 0.5 × PCD (exactly the radius)

blocks.note: For 6 holes, the dividers that scribed the pitch circle step round it exactly six times without being reset: the chord equals the radius.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Equipment
Use
rows: Surface plate (cast iron or granite)
A very flat reference surface to set up and mark work on. Keep it clean and covered; never hammer, cut or weld on it.
Surface gauge (scribing block)
Scribes lines at a set height above the surface plate, parallel to it
Vee blocks
Hold round bar steady, with its axis parallel to the plate, for marking
Angle plate
Holds work at 90° to the surface plate

head: Punch
Point
Use
rows: Prick (dot) punch
Fine, sharp point (often about 30°)
A light mark exactly where lines cross, to locate and check a position; light witness marks along lines
Centre punch
Wider point, usually ground to **90°**
Deepening a checked mark into a dent that guides a drill point
Automatic centre punch
Spring-loaded
Makes a mark when pressed: no hammer needed
Transfer punch
Its body fits the hole; a point in the centre
Passed through an existing hole or template to mark the same position on the part below
Bell (centre-finding) punch
Point centred in a bell-shaped guide
Marks the centre of a round bar's end

blocks.p: Strike punches with a **ball pein hammer** of a light weight. Hold the punch near its point, between your fingers and thumb.

flow: Check the line crossing is correct against the drawing
Tilt the prick punch so you can see its point, and feel it into the exact crossing
Stand the punch upright, keeping the point in place
Tap it once, lightly, with the hammer
Check the mark is exactly on the crossing (a magnifier helps)
Put the centre punch into the mark, stand it upright and tap it to enlarge the dent
If the hole is to be drilled to size, scribe a circle of the hole's size round it with dividers

ul: **Witness marks** are light, evenly spaced punch marks along a cutting line. If the dye or soapstone rubs off, the line can still be seen, and after cutting or filing, half of each mark left on the edge shows that you cut exactly on the line.
A punch mark in the wrong place is hard to remove. Check before you centre punch, not after.
Do not punch hard on thin sheet: it dents and distorts it. Support the sheet on a solid, flat surface.

blocks.note: Wear safety glasses when punching. A punch with a spread, cracked ("mushroom") head must be dressed on a grinder before use: pieces of the head can break off and fly.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Marking out a part, step by step

flow: Read the drawing; check the revision, material, thickness and quantity
Check the plate: right size and material, flat, not damaged
Choose and check the tools: scriber sharp, square true, punch heads sound
Clean the plate, file the burrs off the datum edges, and apply a thin, even coat of marking blue
Mark the datum edges
Scribe the outline lines, measuring every size from the datums
Scribe the hole centre lines, so they cross at each hole centre
Mark angles and chamfers with the square head or protractor
Check every position against the drawing
Prick punch, check, then centre punch the hole centres
Scribe circles and arcs with dividers
Hatch or cross the waste, and add witness marks along cut lines
Check everything again before anything is cut or drilled

blocks.h: Allowances: which side of the line?

ul: Cut on the **waste side** of the line, so the part keeps its full size and you can file back to the line.
Mark the waste with a cross or hatching, so nobody cuts on the wrong side.
Leave room between parts for the **kerf**: about 1 mm for a hacksaw, a few millimetres for a cutting disc or plasma, and more for gas cutting.
Add any allowance the drawing or instructor gives for bending, machining or fitting. Do not add your own without asking.

blocks.p: A bar is 1200 mm long. Five holes are to be equally spaced, with the end holes 50 mm from each end. The distance from the first hole to the last is 1200 − 50 − 50 = 1100 mm, and there are 4 spaces between 5 holes, so the spacing is 1100 ÷ 4 = **275 mm**.
Each position is measured from the datum end (50, 325, 600 …), not by stepping 275 mm from the last hole, so a small error on one hole is not carried to the next.

ul: When many parts are the same, make **one accurate template** (from thin sheet, plate or hardboard), check it carefully against the drawing, and mark it with the job and part number.
Mark round the template, or through its holes with a **transfer punch** or a scriber.
Check the first part marked from the template against the drawing before marking the rest.
Do not copy each new part from the last one cut: errors grow with every copy.

blocks.p: A rectangle with square corners has **equal diagonals**. Measure from corner to corner both ways: if the two diagonals differ, the corners are not square. For hole patterns, measure across opposite hole centres in the same way.

sections.title: Marking out on site: walls, floors and structures

blocks.p: On site you mark large surfaces you cannot scratch, often far from a bench. The tools change, but the principles stay the same: a datum, careful measuring, and checking.

head: Tool
Use
Good practice
rows: Spirit level (600 mm or longer)
Showing whether a line is truly level (horizontal) or plumb (vertical)
Check it end for end; use the longest level that fits
Plumb bob
A pointed weight on a string that hangs truly vertical
Let it stop swinging; shelter it from wind; mark the string's line at top and bottom
Chalk line
Snapping long straight lines between two marks
Stretch it tight, lift it straight out from the surface in the middle, and let go
Laser level
Projecting level and plumb lines across a room
Never look into the beam or point it at anyone's eyes; follow the warning label
Long tape measure
Positions and heights
Measure from the datum line; two people for long runs
Cable and pipe detector
Finding hidden cables, pipes and steel before drilling
Scan the whole area; it is a check, not a guarantee

blocks.h: Setting heights from a datum line

ul: Floors are rarely perfectly level, and ceilings and window heads are often not level either. So all heights are measured from one agreed **level datum line**, not from the floor, the ceiling or a window.
Heights on drawings are often given above the **finished floor level** (written **FFL**), as in "socket outlets 450 mm AFFL" (above finished floor level).
Mark the datum line lightly with a level and pencil (or a laser), then measure each height up or down from it.

flow: Read the layout drawing: positions, heights and spacing
Set a level datum line and agree it with the supervisor
Mark the centre line or edge of each item from the datum and from a fixed starting point
Use the level or plumb bob to get each box or bracket's sides vertical; draw round the box or a template
For a long horizontal run, mark both ends at the right height, snap a chalk line between them and check it with the level
Scan for hidden cables and pipes before drilling
Check every mark against the drawing

blocks.note: Cables usually run straight up, down or across from switches, outlets and fittings. Treat the wall directly above, below and beside them as likely to hide a cable, and scan before you drill there. If the detector finds something where you must drill, stop and ask.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Setting out a square corner: the 3-4-5 method

blocks.p: A triangle with sides of 3, 4 and 5 units always has a right angle (90°) between the 3 and 4 sides. Any multiple works: 0.6 m, 0.8 m and 1.0 m; 1.2 m, 1.6 m and 2.0 m; 3 m, 4 m and 5 m. Use the biggest that fits: it is more accurate.

flow: Mark the corner and run the first side as a straight line
Measure 3 units along the first side from the corner and mark it
Measure 4 units roughly along the second side from the corner
Swing the second side until the distance between the two marks is exactly 5 units
The corner is now square: mark the second side
Complete the rectangle, then check that both diagonals are equal

blocks.p: For a rectangle 2.4 m × 3.2 m, the diagonals should each be **4.0 m** (it is a 3-4-5 triangle with every side × 0.8). If they differ, the shape is not square: adjust until they are equal.

blocks.note: When setting out a steel structure (a carport, a shed or a canopy) on a slab, set the corners and post positions square before any base plate is drilled or fixed. A frame built on corners that are out of square will not fit its roof sheets.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Checking, care of tools, clean-up and reporting

ul: Put the drawing beside the work and re-measure every size from the **same datums** you used.
Check that the lines are fine and clear and that each hole centre is punched exactly where its lines cross.
Count the holes and features, and check their sizes.
Check diagonals of rectangles and hole patterns, and check angles with a square or protractor.
Check that the waste side of each cut line is marked.
For important work, ask a second person or the supervisor to check too.
Clean off the wrong marks, put on fresh marking blue and mark that part again.
If a wrong punch mark cannot be removed, or the material is spoiled, tell the supervisor before going on.
Find the cause (wrong datum, misread size, damaged tool) so it does not happen again.

head: Cause
How a careful worker avoids it
rows: Working from an old drawing
Check the revision before starting
Measuring from the last mark instead of the datum
Measure every size from one datum
Reading the rule from an angle
Eye straight above the mark
Blunt scriber: thick, vague lines
Keep the point sharp
Worn rule end, bent tape hook, square out of true
Check tools before use; report and replace damaged ones
Rushing
Measure twice, check every size at the end

blocks.h: Care and storage of marking out tools

ul: Wipe each tool clean of dirt, chalk and marking dye after use.
Put a thin film of light oil on steel tools: warm, damp and salty air rusts them quickly.
Store rules, squares, dividers and calipers in a box, drawer or rack, where they cannot be dropped or knocked.
Keep caps on scriber and divider points.
Use each tool only for its own job: never use a rule as a screwdriver or a square as a hammer.
Keep tapes closed and dry, and do not let the blade snap back.
Have mushroomed punch heads dressed, and blunt scribers and punches sharpened, by a competent person.
Label a damaged or inaccurate tool and report it, so it is repaired or replaced.

blocks.h: At the end of the job

flow: Check the marked parts are complete; label them with the job number or part name and which way up they go
Hand them over, or put them where the supervisor says
Put the lid on the marking blue and store it away from heat and sparks
Put dye- or solvent-soaked rags in the closed metal bin
Clean, oil and store the tools, with caps on the points
Sweep up filings and offcuts; scrap in the scrap bin; on site, clear chalk lines, tape and pins
Report damaged tools and short or spoiled material, and note them on the job sheet

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise with your instructor.

ul: I can read a drawing for marking out: revision, sizes, units, material, quantity and datums.
I can explain what a datum is and why every size is measured from it.
I can name the hazards of marking out and how to control them.
I can choose measuring, marking and squaring tools and check that they are accurate.
I can read a steel rule and tape measure correctly.
I can prepare a surface and choose the right marking method for bright steel, black steel, galvanised sheet, aluminium, walls and floors.
I can mark lines, angles and chamfers, find the centre of a bar and scribe circles with dividers or trammels.
I can mark equally spaced holes on a pitch circle.
I can prick punch and centre punch accurately and add witness marks.
I can mark the waste side, allow for the kerf and use a template for repeated parts.
I can set out level, plumb and straight lines on site from a datum line and check for hidden services.
I can set out a square corner with the 3-4-5 method and check a rectangle with its diagonals.
I can check my marking out, correct mistakes, care for and store the tools, and report problems.

c1.title: Canopy base plates in St Ann's Bay
c1.text: Damion is marking out twelve base plates, each 200 × 200 × 10 mm, for the posts of a shop canopy in St Ann's Bay, St Ann. Each plate needs four Ø18 holes on 140 mm square centres, 30 mm in from each edge. The plates were cut on a guillotine, and their cut edges still carry burrs. He plans to drill one plate first and use it as a template for the others.

c2.title: A pump flange in Frankfield
c2.text: Kenisha is marking out a flange for a water pump at a farm workshop in Frankfield, Clarendon. The flange is a Ø200 disc of 10 mm steel with six bolt holes equally spaced on a 150 mm PCD. She has scribed the centre lines and the pitch circle, and is about to step the hole positions round the circle with her dividers. Her centre punch has just been dressed, and she also has a prick punch.

c3.title: Outlets and trunking in a Highgate classroom
c3.text: Shamar, an Electrical Installation trainee, is working with his supervisor, Ms Morrison, in a classroom at a school in Highgate, St Mary. He must mark four outlet boxes at 450 mm above finished floor level and a trunking run 5.5 m long at 1200 mm, along a newly painted block wall. The floor falls about 15 mm from one end of the wall to the other. He has a 1 m spirit level, a laser level, a chalk line, a tape, a plumb bob and a cable detector.

c4.title: Setting out a shed in Junction
c4.text: Oneil and Shanelle are setting out the corners of a steel storage shed, 2.4 m × 3.2 m, on a new concrete slab in Junction, St Elizabeth, using a tape, string lines, steel pins and chalk. When they have marked all four corners, they measure the two diagonals: one is 4.03 m and the other 3.97 m.

c5.title: Putting away at a Kingston workshop
c5.text: At the end of a marking out job at a workshop in Kingston, Kadeem notices that the first 5 mm of his steel rule is worn round. When he scribes a line with the try square, turns it over and scribes again from the same point, the two lines spread apart. The tin of marking blue is still open on the bench next to the grinding area, and two rags soaked in dye lie beside it.

questions.q: Before Damion uses two plate edges as his datums, what should he do to them?
o: Paint them a bright colour so that they are easy to see
Nothing, as guillotined edges are always true
Grind a bevel along them for the welds
File off the burrs so the square and rule sit true
questions.why: A burr holds the stock of the square or the end of the rule away from the true edge, so every size measured from it is wrong. Clean, straight, square datum edges come first.

questions.q: After marking the four hole centres on 140 mm square centres, what should the distance be between diagonally opposite holes?
o: About 140 mm
About 170 mm
About 198 mm
About 280 mm
questions.why: The diagonal of a 140 mm square is 140 × 1.414 ≈ 198 mm. Measuring both diagonals checks that the hole pattern is square, just as for a rectangle.

questions.q: With the first plate drilled as a template, how should Damion mark the holes on the other eleven plates?
o: Clamp the template on and mark through each hole with a transfer punch
Measure each new plate again from its own edges and punch the centres
Copy each plate from the plate he marked just before it
Drill through the template and the plate below in one go, without marking
questions.why: A transfer punch fits the template's hole and marks its exact centre on the plate beneath. One checked template gives identical plates; copying from the last plate lets errors grow.

questions.q: Why should Damion check the first plate marked from the template before marking the rest?
o: To find out how long the job will take him
To prove the template gives the drawing's sizes
To see whether the marking dye has dried well enough
To warm up the punch before the main batch
questions.why: Any error in the template is repeated on every plate. Checking the first copy against the drawing catches it before twelve plates are spoiled.

questions.q: To step six equal holes round the 150 mm PCD, what should Kenisha set her dividers to?
o: 75 mm
60 mm
50 mm
150 mm
questions.why: For six holes the chord between neighbours equals the radius of the pitch circle: 150 ÷ 2 = 75 mm. The setting that scribed the circle steps round it exactly six times.

questions.q: After six steps, the dividers land about 3 mm past Kenisha's first mark. What should she do?
o: Squeeze the extra 3 mm into the gap between the last two holes
Open the dividers by 3 mm and step round again
Close the dividers by about 0.5 mm and step round again
Accept it, since 3 mm is very small on a flange
questions.why: The 3 mm error has built up over six steps, so each step is about 0.5 mm too long. Close the dividers slightly and step round again until the last step lands on the first mark.

questions.q: Why should Kenisha make each hole mark with the prick punch before the centre punch?
o: The centre punch will not dent steel without a prick mark first
The light, fine mark can be checked before it is made deeper
Prick punch marks are deep enough to drill from directly
Using both punches makes the hole come out larger
questions.why: The fine point of the prick punch is easy to place exactly on the line crossing, and a light mark can still be corrected. Only when it is right is it enlarged with the 90° centre punch.

questions.q: Why would measuring each box height up from the floor give a poor result in this classroom?
o: Floors are always measured in inches on site
The tape would have to bend into the corner of the wall
The boxes would end up too close to the ceiling
The floor falls, so the boxes would step out of level
questions.why: Measured from a sloping floor, the boxes and trunking would follow the slope. A single level datum line on the wall, with every height measured from it, keeps them all level.

questions.q: Shamar checks the spirit level by reading it, turning it end for end on the same spot, and reading again. The bubble sits differently the second time. What does this tell him?
o: The wall is not straight
The level is out of true
The spot is not quite level
The floor is not level
questions.why: On the same spot, an accurate level reads the same both ways round. A different reading means the vial is out of adjustment: the level must not be used until it is put right or replaced.

questions.q: How should Shamar mark the box outlines on the newly painted wall?
o: Scratch them with a scriber so they last
Draw them lightly with a sharp pencil
Draw them with a thick permanent marker
Snap a red chalk line through each box
questions.why: Pencil marks lightly made can be wiped off or painted over. A scratch or permanent ink spoils the finish, and some coloured chalks stain.

questions.q: The detector signals about 100 mm to the side of where one box is to go. What should Shamar do?
o: Drill a little to one side of the signal
Drill slowly so that he feels any pipe first
Stop and tell Ms Morrison before drilling
Ignore it, as detectors often give false alarms
questions.why: The signal may be a live cable or a water pipe. Drilling into either is dangerous. Stop, report it, and let the supervisor decide whether to move the box or trace the service.

questions.q: If every corner were square, what would each diagonal measure?
questions.why: 2.4 m and 3.2 m are 3 and 4 multiplied by 0.8, so the diagonal is 5 × 0.8 = 4.0 m. 5.6 m is just the two sides added together.

questions.q: What do the diagonals of 4.03 m and 3.97 m tell Oneil and Shanelle?
o: The tape has stretched in the sun
The shed is the right size, so carry on
The slab is not level, so it must be packed
The corners are out of square: adjust them
questions.why: A rectangle with square corners has equal diagonals. A 60 mm difference means the shape is skewed, so they move the corners until both diagonals are equal (about 4.0 m).

questions.q: To set out the first corner square with their tape, which set of measurements could they use?
questions.why: 1.2, 1.6 and 2.0 m are 3, 4 and 5 multiplied by 0.4, so they form a right angle. The other sets are not in the ratio 3 : 4 : 5.

questions.q: Until the rule is replaced, how should Kadeem measure with it accurately?
o: Start from the worn end and add 5 mm to every reading
Hold it at an angle so the end is not used
Start from the end and take off 5 mm
Measure from the 10 mm line and take off 10 mm
questions.why: A worn end gives a false zero. Measuring from a clear graduation such as 10 mm, and subtracting it, avoids the worn part. The rule should still be reported.

questions.q: What does the try square test show?
o: The square is out of true
The bench is not flat enough
The scriber needs sharpening
The lines need marking blue
questions.why: Turning the square over doubles any error. If the two lines spread apart, the blade is not at 90° to the stock: label the square and report it.

questions.q: What should Kadeem do with the marking blue and the rags?
o: Keep the open tin by the grinder ready for tomorrow, and hang the rags over the bench to dry out
Leave the tin open so it dries out, and throw the rags into the general waste bin
Put the lid on the tin and store it away from heat and sparks; rags into the closed metal bin
Pour the rest of the dye down the sink, and burn the rags in the yard
questions.why: The dye and its vapour are flammable, and grinding sparks can ignite them. Closed, stored away from heat, with dye-soaked rags in a closed metal bin, they cannot start a fire.

questions.q: Nikki is marking a bend line on aluminium sheet that will be folded to 90°. Which marking method is best?
o: A deep scribed line, so it is easy to see
A fine marker or pencil line
A row of centre punch marks along it
A line cut with the corner of a file
questions.why: A scratch, punch mark or file nick on a bend line can start a crack when aluminium is folded. A fine marker or pencil line shows the bend without damaging the surface.

questions.q: Five holes are to be equally spaced along a 1200 mm bar, with the end holes 50 mm from each end. What is the spacing between hole centres?
o: 220 mm
240 mm
300 mm
275 mm
questions.why: From the first hole to the last is 1200 − 100 = 1100 mm, and five holes have four spaces: 1100 ÷ 4 = 275 mm. Mark each from the datum end: 50, 325, 600, 875 and 1150 mm.

questions.q: Kayla must mark the centre of the end of a 50 mm round bar, but the centre head is missing. Which method works?
o: Scribe four arcs from the edge with odd-leg calipers at about 25 mm
Measure 25 mm in from one point on the edge and punch it
Draw one line right across the end with a rule and punch at its middle point
Set dividers to 50 mm and scribe one circle round the edge
questions.why: Arcs scribed from points round the edge, with the calipers set to about the radius, make a small shape whose middle is the centre. A single measurement from one point does not find the centre.
